item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
There is a way to conclusively determine if the discs are pre-recorded or not.
Compare the data on a disc before and after it is watched.
The unbreakable copy-protection doesn't prevent examining (or even duplicating) the raw data and taking note of any post-play differences.
Changes=ghost in the machine; no changes=time traveler and/or very accurate precognition.

Of course, that isn't really the point is it?
The real meat here is that I spent the whole time reading thinking of various ways to prove or disprove the nature of this thing. Only to find the test log and interviews addressing each experiment almost as I came up with them. It was a very surreal experience; a bit like what I imagine talking to the discman must be like.

This is the most immersive skip I can recall ever coming across.
I am bummed that this seems to be KenLeo's only contribution to the site.

item.title: Re: Safe?
item.content:encoded:
Object class is difficulty of containment, not the amount we know about the item. Reference the "locked-box" test:

Safe-class items can be thrown in a locked box and forgotten, and nothing will happen with them.

Euclid-class items we're unsure what will happen if we leave them in a locked box, or we've tried to leave them and weird though not enormously damaging stuff happened.

Keter-class items will eat the box, the box's guards, and breach the masquerade.

Thaumiel-class items are the box.

item.title: Safe?
item.content:encoded:
Does this one really count as a "safe" SCP?

The Foundation knows absolutely nothing about whatever made the discs, or the "entity" that may or may not reside within them. The discs themselves may be secured with very little chance of them escaping on their own, but they know nothing about whatever is causing them to behave like they do.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Doesn't make sense to me.
As soon as they found out that it shares knowledge between instances, it became a security breach.
After all, they admit there are more copies out there, loose.
And anything it can gleen from the staff, it can relay to outside forces.
For all they know, there could be an agency manufacturing them, and having each copy report on the staff and testing proceedures of the Foundation.
Furthermore, it can see the color of the TV it is played on. And it shows a willingness to withhold data.
For all they know it has full knowledge of the entire room, or even the base it is played at.

The risk is just too high to allow testing anywhere but at a secluded base. And even then, the objective would not be to find its capabilities, but rather who made it, and where the rest of the copies are, to seal the breach.
